{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call-2c0f7d1f-c04b-4f17-b656-98314d061a02-3","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t---\n2\tname: harbor-task-creator\n3\tdescription: \"Create Harbor evaluation tasks from scratch. Generates task.toml configuration, instruction.md for agents, environment/Dockerfile setup, tests/test.sh verification scripts, and solution/solve.sh reference solutions. Use this skill whenever creating, scaffolding, or authoring new Harbor benchmark tasks, evaluation environments, or agent challenges. Also use when fixing broken tasks, debugging reward file issues, or structuring multi-container evaluation environments.\"\n4\t---\n5\t\n6\t# Creating Harbor Evaluation Tasks\n7\t\n8\tHarbor tasks are self-contained evaluation challenges for AI agents. Each task provides an instruction, a sandboxed Docker environment, automated tests, and optionally a reference solution. Understanding how Harbor wires these pieces together at runtime is key to writing tasks that work correctly.\n9\t\n10\t## Quick Start\n11\t\n12\tScaffold a new task with the CLI:\n13\t\n14\t```bash\n15\tharbor tasks init my-task\n16\t# Flags:\n17\t#   --tasks-dir (-p)              Parent directory (default: current dir)\n18\t#   --no-pytest                   Use plain bash tests instead of pytest template\n19\t#   --no-solution                 Skip generating solution/solve.sh\n20\t#   --include-canary-strings      Embed tracking GUIDs in generated files\n21\t#   --metadata-template <path>    Seed task.toml [metadata] from a .toml template\n22\t```\n23\t\n24\tTo convert Terminal Bench tasks to Harbor format: `harbor tasks migrate -i <tb-tasks/> -o <harbor-tasks/>`\n25\t\n26\tOr create the directory structure manually:\n27\t\n28\t```\n29\tmy-task/\n30\t├── task.toml              # Configuration (timeouts, resources, metadata)\n31\t├── instruction.md         # Natural language prompt for the agent\n32\t├── environment/\n33\t│   ├── Dockerfile         # Container image definition\n34\t│   ├── docker-compose.yaml  # Multi-container setup (optional)\n35\t│   └── ...                # Files COPYed into the image\n36\t├── tests/\n37\t│   ├── test.sh            # Verification entry point (required)\n38\t│   └── test_*.py          # Pytest files (optional)\n39\t├── solution/\n40\t│   └── solve.sh           # Reference solution (optional)\n41\t└── README.md              # Human documentation (optional)\n42\t```\n43\t\n44\t**Required files:** `task.toml`, `instruction.md`, `environment/` (with Dockerfile or docker-compose.yaml), `tests/test.sh`.\n45\t\n46\t**Validation:** Harbor validates tasks by checking that `task.toml`, `environment/`, `instruction.md`, and `tests/test.sh` all exist (via `TaskPaths.is_valid()`).\n47\t\n48\tRun the AI-powered quality checker after creating a task:\n49\t\n50\t```bash\n51\tharbor tasks check ./my-task    # LLM-based rubric assessment\n52\t```\n53\t\n54\t## How Harbor Executes a Task (Runtime Model)\n55\t\n56\tUnderstanding the runtime flow prevents most common authoring mistakes:\n57\t\n58\t1. **Build** — Harbor builds the Docker image from `environment/Dockerfile` (or starts compose services from `environment/docker-compose.yaml`).\n59\t2. **Mount** — Three host directories are bind-mounted into the container:\n60\t   - `/logs/verifier/` — where test.sh writes reward files and stdout\n61\t   - `/logs/agent/` — agent logs\n62\t   - `/logs/artifacts/` — any artifacts\n63\t3. **Agent runs** — The agent connects to the container, reads instruction.md (provided separately, not in the container), and works in the environment.\n64\t4. **Upload tests** — After the agent finishes, Harbor uploads `tests/` to `/tests/` inside the container using `docker compose cp`.\n65\t5. **Execute test.sh** — Harbor runs `chmod +x /tests/test.sh` then executes it. Working directory is `/tests/`. Each task provides an instruction, a sandboxed Docker environment, automated tests, and optionally a reference solution. Understanding how Harbor wires these pieces together at runtime is key to writing tasks that work correctly.\n\n## Quick Start\n\nScaffold a new task with the CLI:\n\n```bash\nharbor tasks init my-task\n# Flags:\n#   --tasks-dir (-p)              Parent directory (default: current dir)\n#   --no-pytest                   Use plain bash tests instead of pytest template\n#   --no-solution                 Skip generating solution/solve.sh\n#   --include-canary-strings      Embed tracking GUIDs in generated files\n#   --metadata-template <path>    Seed task.toml [metadata] from a .toml template\n```\n\nTo convert Terminal Bench tasks to Harbor format: `harbor tasks migrate -i <tb-tasks/> -o <harbor-tasks/>`\n\nOr create the directory structure manually:\n\n```\nmy-task/\n├── task.toml              # Configuration (timeouts, resources, metadata)\n├── instruction.md         # Natural language prompt for the agent\n├── environment/\n│   ├── Dockerfile         # Container image definition\n│   ├── docker-compose.yaml  # Multi-container setup (optional)\n│   └── ...                # Files COPYed into the image\n├── tests/\n│   ├── test.sh            # Verification entry point (required)\n│   └── test_*.py          # Pytest files (optional)\n├── solution/\n│   └── solve.sh           # Reference solution (optional)\n└── README.md              # Human documentation (optional)\n```\n\n**Required files:** `task.toml`, `instruction.md`, `environment/` (with Dockerfile or docker-compose.yaml), `tests/test.sh`.\n\n**Validation:** Harbor validates tasks by checking that `task.toml`, `environment/`, `instruction.md`, and `tests/test.sh` all exist (via `TaskPaths.is_valid()`).\n\nRun the AI-powered quality checker after creating a task:\n\n```bash\nharbor tasks check ./my-task    # LLM-based rubric assessment\n```\n\n## How Harbor Executes a Task (Runtime Model)\n\nUnderstanding the runtime flow prevents most common authoring mistakes:\n\n1. **Build** — Harbor builds the Docker image from `environment/Dockerfile` (or starts compose services from `environment/docker-compose.yaml`).\n2. **Mount** — Three host directories are bind-mounted into the container:\n   - `/logs/verifier/` — where test.sh writes reward files and stdout\n   - `/logs/agent/` — agent logs\n   - `/logs/artifacts/` — any artifacts\n3. **Agent runs** — The agent connects to the container, reads instruction.md (provided separately, not in the container), and works in the environment.\n4. **Upload tests** — After the agent finishes, Harbor uploads `tests/` to `/tests/` inside the container using `docker compose cp`.\n5. **Execute test.sh** — Harbor runs `chmod +x /tests/test.sh` then executes it. Working directory is `/tests/`. Environment variables from `[verifier].env` in task.toml are injected.\n6. **Parse reward** — Harbor reads `/logs/verifier/reward.txt` (priority) or `/logs/verifier/reward.json`. If neither exists, the trial errors with `RewardFileNotFoundError`.\n\nThis means: the agent never sees `tests/` or `solution/`. Tests run after the agent is done. Reward files must always be written.\n\n## Writing instruction.md\n\nThe instruction is the only thing the agent sees. It must be completely self-contained.\n\n**Guidelines:**\n- Specify exact file paths the agent should create or modify (e.g., \"Write your answer to `/app/output.txt`\")\n- State the expected output format precisely (JSON schema, line format, etc.)\n- Include all necessary context — the agent cannot ask clarifying questions\n- Do NOT mention tests, scoring, or evaluation mechanics\n- Do NOT leak file paths from `tests/` or `solution/`\n- If the task requires structured data output, document the exact schema in the instruction — the quality checker flags this\n\n**Anti-patterns to avoid:**\n- \"Submit your answer\" — agents don't submit; they write files that tests check\n- \"You may use any approach\" — too vague; specify constraints when they matter\n- Referencing files outside the environment (agents only see the container)\n- Describing behavior in the instruction that isn't actually tested (and vice versa)\n\n**Example:**\n\n```markdown\n# Fix the Sorting Bug\n\nThe file `/app/sort.py` contains a merge sort implementation with a bug\nthat causes incorrect results on arrays with duplicate elements.\n\nFix the bug so that `sort_array()` correctly sorts any list of integers.\nThe fix should be in `/app/sort.py`. Do not rename the function.\n```\n\n## Configuring task.toml\n\nThe task.toml file controls timeouts, resources, metadata, and MCP server configuration. It is parsed by `TaskConfig.model_validate_toml()`.\n\n**Minimal example:**\n\n```toml\nversion = \"1.0\"\n\n[metadata]\ndifficulty = \"easy\"\ncategory = \"programming\"\n\n[agent]\ntimeout_sec = 300.0\n\n[verifier]\ntimeout_sec = 120.0\n```\n\n**Full configuration — see [references/task-toml-reference.md](references/task-toml-reference.md) for every field, type, and default.**\n\nKey sections:\n- `[metadata]` — free-form dict; conventional keys: difficulty, category, tags, author info, time estimates\n- `[agent]` — `timeout_sec` (float, default 600.0): wall-clock seconds for the agent\n- `[verifier]` — `timeout_sec` (float, default 600.0) and `env` (dict): timeout and environment variables for test.sh\n- `[environment]` — resource limits (cpus, memory_mb, storage_mb, gpus), pre-built images, network access, MCP servers\n- `[solution]` — `env` (dict): environment variables for solve.sh\n- `[[environment.mcp_servers]]` — MCP server configs (repeated section with `[[double brackets]]`)\n\n**MCP server configuration** (for tasks that provide MCP tools to the agent):\n\n```toml\n[[environment.mcp_servers]]\nname = \"my-mcp-server\"\ntransport = \"streamable-http\"       # What this means is that Redis provides access to mutable data structures via a set of commands, which are sent using a *server-client* model with TCP sockets and a simple protocol. So different processes can query and modify the same data structures in a shared way.\n7\t\n8\tData structures implemented into Redis have a few special properties:\n9\t\n10\t* Redis cares to store them on disk, even if they are always served and modified into the server memory. This means that Redis is fast, but that it is also non-volatile.\n11\t* The implementation of data structures emphasizes memory efficiency, so data structures inside Redis will likely use less memory compared to the same data structure modelled using a high-level programming language.\n12\t* Redis offers a number of features that are natural to find in a database, like replication, tunable levels of durability, clustering, and high availability.\n13\t\n14\tAnother good example is to think of Redis as a more complex version of memcached, where the operations are not just SETs and GETs, but operations that work with complex data types like Lists, Sets, ordered data structures, and so forth.\n15\t\n16\tIf you want to know more, this is a list of selected starting points:\n17\t\n18\t* The union rule helps, but it still leaves us with a choice: should we ship a pre-built binary for convenience or keep the source pristine so the agent can demonstrate its build skills?\n\nMy take is to ship the source in a writable workdir, install the minimal toolchain (gcc, make, libc-dev, pkg-config, openssl-dev), and let the agent handle compilation. That way we satisfy build-system, repair/debugging, and configuration tasks without pre-building anything the task might ask to rebuild. No pre-built binaries, no test-only deps like pytest or jq. Redis.conf stays in the source tree for configuration tasks.\n\nHere's the Dockerfile and setup.sh:\n\n```dockerfile\nFROM ubuntu:24.04\n\nENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive\n\nRUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \\\n    ca-certificates git \\\n    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists\n\n # Clone Redis at pinned commit\nRUN git clone https://github.com/redis/redis /src \\\n    && git -C /src checkout 335554f18caf7bbf6b0ac2b3548133d750f00a1b\n\nCOPY setup.sh setup-overlay.sh smoke_test.sh /opt/env # smoke_test.sh is optional\nCOPY assets/ /data/  # empty assets dir is fine\n\nRUN bash /opt/env/setup.sh\nRUN bash /opt/env/setup-overlay.sh\n\nWORKDIR /app\n```\n\nAnd setup.sh:\n\n```bash\n#!/usr/bin/env bash\nset -euo pipefail\n\nexport DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive\n\napt-get update\napt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \\\n    build-essential \\\n    pkg-config \\\n    libssl-dev \\\n    tcl8.6 \\\n    tclx \\\n    procps \\\n    time \\\n    ca-certificates \\\n    git\n rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*\n\n# Create directories\nmkdir -p /app /data /results\ncp -a /src/. /app/  # copy source to writable workdir\nchmod -R a+rwX /app /data /results\n\n# Don't build Redis\n```\n\nsmoke_test can verify the toolchain and that make can parse without modifying source.\n\nThis keeps the base general, lets the agent build when needed, and provides the baseline for performance tasks. Redis binaries are not\n# pre-built so later build-system tasks still have work to do.\ncommand -v gcc >/dev/null || fail \"gcc missing\"\ncommand -v make >/dev/null || fail \"make missing\"\ncommand -v pkg-config >/dev/null || fail \"pkg-config missing\"\ngcc --version >/dev/null || fail \"gcc --version failed\"\nmake --version >/dev/null || fail \"make --version failed\"\n\n# A declared repo entrypoint actually runs: runtest without args prints usage\n# and exits non-zero, so invoke tclsh on the helper with --help-style flags\n# that do not start the suite. `make -C /app -n` is a live Makefile parse.\nmake -C \"${WORKDIR}\" -n all >/dev/null || fail \"make -n all failed\"\n\n# Confirm the clone at /src is still at the pinned commit (read-only check).\nif [ -d /src/.git ]; then\n    pinned=\"335554f18caf7bbf6b0ac2b3548133d750f00a1b\"\n    actual=\"$(git -C /src rev-parse HEAD)\"\n    [ \"$actual\" = \"$pinned\" ] || fail \"commit mismatch: $actual != $pinned\"\nfi\n\n# Do not leave any source-tree dirt.\nif git -C \"${WORKDIR}\" status --porcelain 2>/dev/null | grep -q .; then\n    fail \"workdir source was modified\"\nfi\n\necho \"SMOKE_OK\"\nexit 0\n"}}],"model":"grok-4.6","stop_reason":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":0,"output_tokens":0,"cache_creation_input_tokens":0,"cache_read_input_tokens":0},"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"d702b785-ea3e-4395-90c8-12224f1439fc","uuid":"c4fe8ee2-5eda-426e-95f4-585d1261abbe","timestamp":"2026-09-18T05:39:44.238Z"}
